Leading by Example

By: Este de Klerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
SA has a youth unemployment rate of 60%,third highest in the world. Change doesn't happen overnight, but at least one organisation is trying to change the values of learners to become future leaders

Summary:
SA has a youth unemployment rate of 60%, the third highest in the world. Change doesn't happen overnight, but at least one organisation is trying to change the values of learners to become future leaders.

In 2011, we did a story about Columba1400SA - an Academy that teaches young people to change the way they think. This leadership development program was founded by high-profile Scottish cleric and leadership Norman Drummond in Scotland in 1997 and brought to South Africa in 2009 by businessman Rob Taylor. When we did the story in 2011, they have had 350 learners who graduated successfully under this programme introduced into mostly rural and disadvantaged schools, working on a selection system. Now they already have 3500 graduates.

Further information:
Too many young people drop out before completing high school, not having something to look forward to after completing school. Most of them that do complete matric, leave ill-prepared for life after school and more often than not, become part of the 60% unemployment statistic for young people between the ages of 18 and 35. A lack of skills and a good value system while in school contribute to this high youth unemployment figure. Unemployment traps people in poverty and potentially also contribute to instability in the country.

Columba 1400SA has a mission to build a national movement of engaged young leaders for youth employment and school improvement and they offer a values-based leadership programme to schools that challenge learners, not only to become the best they can be, to think out of the box,. to have a future vision, to be motivated and determined, but also to inspire others and lead by example in getting a society together in order to uplift their own communities.

The system works on selective basis. Learners have to write essays on the changes they want to see in themselves, their community and their schools. High-achievers and troublemakers are included in the mix and taught values such as perseverance, creativity, relationship and leadership, planning and problem solving, managing feelings, resilience and determination and integrity to elevate their ideals in life beyond just self-interest to examine projects with social and environmental significance.

Columba activate the potential of a small core group of learners and adults (the principal and educators, maybe some adults in the community) to lead positive change. This group in turn spend two years recruiting, mobilising and engaging large numbers of their peers and implementing ongoing social impact projects and these projects provide numerous opportunities for learners to develop a range of skills and capabilities.

75% of the Columba graduates being tracked are in higher of further education programmes studying or working within two years of leaving school.

Columba's mission is to activate a national movement of engaged young leaders to improve their schools and youth employment. In six years, Columba has developed more than 2400 leaders in 90 schools in seven provinces. They have mobilised over 40 000 beneficiaries with 21st century skills, such as foundational literacies (how students apply core skills to everyday tasks like literacy, numeracy, scientific literacy, ICT literacy, financial literacy and cultural and civic literacy), competencies (how students approach complex challenges like critical thinking and problem solving, creativity, communication and collaboration) and character qualities (how students approach their changing environment like curiosity, initiative, persistence/grit, adaptability, leadership and social and cultural awareness).

The impact on the individual is that that learner is more future orientated, inspired for education, self-confident and committed to social contribution. 81% of Columba graduates are studying with the help of bursaries, working or volunteering after leaving school - ultimately narrowing the gap of South Africa's 60% young unemployment rate for people between the ages of 18 and 35.

The effect these changes value systems and endorsed programmes have on schools are enormously successful - of participating principals, 100% report improved culture of learning in the school, 90% report it made their role and that of other educators easier and 100% would recommend the program to other schools for its relevance and empowering outcomes. In schools there is a strong positive impact on academic performance, school drop-outs, teen pregnancy, classroom discipline, late coming and absenteeism.

In the 2011 story, we introduced the Columba 1400SA programme to our viewers. Although we will still be saying in this story what Columba is and what they do and still go to three schools in Thaba Nchu outside Bloemfontein where we will speak to one very inspiring learner at one of Thaba Nchu's more rural schools (she is making a massive impact on her school and community as an individual, but also as part of her small group), we will be speaking to a principal and teacher at another school in Thaba Nchu where the results over the past years have been enormous and at another school in Thaba Nchu, we will be focusing on the small group of learners who are part of the Columba programme and making huge strides in their community - they even started a feeding scheme for the primary school, getting their own sponsors and the Free State education department followed on and is now providing this Primary School with a feeding scheme every day.

In Johannesburg we will be interviewing the CEO of Columba on the changes since our last story and the impact they are making, and we will interview two Columba Alumni's - Caroline, who has had a complete 360 turn-around in her life because of the Columba leadership programme in 2011 and is now studying chemical engineering, and Solly, who became involved in gansterism before he even turned ten, and also had a complete turnaround in his life because of the programme - he said he only wanted to join Columba to make trouble, then realised what he could make of his life. He graduated matric with four distinctions, is now working at a FET college and studying law through Unisa.

The three learners we have interviewed in our 2011 story, are all three still based in KZN. I will only mention in the new story what they do now and where they work - how their lives have progressed since.

Press Release:


Birthing Leaders
The country’s youth unemployment rate – at a whopping 49 percent – is one of the highest in the world. While many young South Africans face a bleak future, opportunities to discover potential in the ashes of desperation abound. And that’s exactly what Columba Leadership Academy – with its focus on rural and disadvantaged schools – has done, producing over 3500 future leaders from youngsters whose lives were destined to be a struggle.


Script:


LEADING BY EXAMPLE SCRIPT

PRODUCER: ESTé DE KLERK

RELEBOGILE: I want to be a teacher. Reason being, I had a wonderful teacher who always seems inspiring.
THEMBELIHLE: I want to serve a footprint that everyone could follow. When I die I want them to say "she was a legend" and after my matric I want to study at the university doing medicine. I want to be a medical detective.

Dreams of a bright future for two learners on the brink of entering a new phase in their lives…
Bright futures that might be hindered without having the necessary financial resources to further their education.
A reality faced by thousands of students…

DEVI LINK: The feesmustfall campaign was a reminder that young South Africans do have a voice and that when they organise themselves it is a powerful voice which cannot be ignored.

[CB 31 OCTOBER 2014/FEESMUSTFALL: Students across the country have stood together in a way we haven’t seen since the 1980’s. The protest has raged from WITS University to Rhodes to the gates of Parliament to the Union Buildings. People are talking about an African Spring – a tipping point in South Africa.]

DEVI LINK: This is Thaba Nchu, east of Bloemfontein. Unemployment is rife here, bringing with it domestic violence, substance abuse and other serious issues. The future here for young children is not too bright.

Eighteen-year old Thembelihle Stuurman lives here with her aunt, sister and three-year old niece in a two-roomed shack.
Like most people in this township, they’re living hand to mouth.

THEMBELIHLE STUURMAN: I grew up in Gauteng. When I was six years my father passed away and life wasn't really good at home. In 2012 - I was twelve years old - she also passed away. So, I'm an orphan.

DEVI: How did you get here to Thaba Nchu? THEMBELIHLE: I was living with my brothers and I felt as if I needed a mother or someone who'd give me that mother's love. So I had to move and come here.
Besides being a grade 11-learner at the Christian Liphoko Secondary School and having to study hard in order to apply for bursaries, she’s also responsible for the household chores.

But she’s not despondent.
Thembelihle is one of the fortunate learners who was selected to be part of the Columba Leadership Academy - a values-based programme that brings hope through real change in economically disadvantaged schools in the country.

THEMBELIHLE: I felt so excited. I was ready to take on the adventure and go and study new things.

In 2011, we brought you the story of how the Columba Leadership Academy change the way learners think through values such as perseverance, creativity, integrity and service.

[CB 2011: This leadership development program was founded by high-profile Scottish cleric and leadership expert Norman Drummond in Scotland in 1997 and brought to South Africa in 2009 by businessman Rob Taylor.]

A group of twelve grade 10-learners – from high-achievers to troublemakers – are chosen from each school by a selection process through essays they have to write about the change they want to see within themselves their schools and their communities.

The 12 learners and three teachers then go on a six-day course where these values are taught and discussed.

[CB 2011: ROB TAYLOR: If you live in a shack, it is hard to see opportunity in that environment, so we take them out into a lodge in a game reserve, a beautiful place that shows a place of openness and possibility and that combined with the experience you learn of values, has a profound impact.]

Columba CEO, Tracy Hackland, says the learners are then challenged to go back to their schools to mobilise and lead their peers for the next two years in bringing about change by initiating and implementing improvement projects.

TRACY HACKLAND: Columba starts the process and then the young people, the principal and the educators pick it up from there.

So, once the learners own and implement the values, change happens naturally and the success of the program is multiplied.

It has now been introduced in a hundred-and-five schools in six provinces.
These young people are taking control of their own destinies and not waiting for others to take that first step.

MRS MARY RANCHO: These are young children but they can think twice as we are thinking as adults.

Mary Rancho was appointed at Christian Liphoko Secondary School in Thaba Nchu in 2013 to change around the then dysfunctional school.
She quickly realised the potential of the leadership program.

MRS MARY RANCHO: These learners are giving a lot of support to the school. Actually, I will say they are part of the management of the school.

Mary says the Columba learners are leading by example.

MRS RANCHO: We are also using them to talk to their peers. You know, when one learner is talking to another learner they understand better, so they are the ones who made these learners to change their attitudes and to say: "We are no longer going back, we are moving forward.”
Not only have the learners improved academically – the school’s matric pass rate increased from 61% in 2012 to 85% in 2015 – but they’re also bringing change in their school and community.

TRACY HACKLAND: So, it's not a case of waiting for the resources, it's a case of starting, doing whatever they can do bring change. It's audacious and they're doing it from a spirit of really wanting to improve their communities.

At their own school they created a school library and started a vegetable garden that wouldn’t only supplement the Education Department’s feeding scheme, but vegetables will also be given to the community.

Through raising funds, they also started a feeding scheme for the local primary school.
And Mary says she was astonished by their initiative and perseverance to raise funds for a dental project.

MRS RANCHO: they decided to phone a company in Bloemfontein. they were informed that they had to pay a sum of almost eleven thousand for the project for a primary school and they said "just give us a week. I was so amazed. In six days days’ time, they were able to collect eleven thousand.

Perseverance is all it really takes, says twenty-year old Sibusiso Molteno.
He grew up in Alexandra township and saw gangsters as he role models before he changed his life around through the Columba program.

He now studies law with a full scholarship at WITS.

SIBU: Not everyone will get the chance to be part of Columba.
It’s all about passion. Start by setting your own goals. Be specific and realistic.

This, Sibusiso believes, is one of the only ways in which the country’s high youth unemployment rate could be curbed.

DEVI LINK: According to STATS SA, South Africa has a youth unemployment rate of 49% for youth between the ages of 15 and 24. That is one of the worst statistics in the world.

SIBU: For me my drive is the township that I come from. If I wasn’t for that township, I doubt whether I would be the person that I am today.

In giving back to his community, Sibu and 34 other student volunteers offer their time on a Saturday to tutor grade 10, 11 and 12 learners from Secondary Schools in Alex.

And to the learners, he is a role model, says Zama Ndlovu.

ZAMA NDLOVU: We want to be like him and also want to help kids and not be selfish like other people. I would go for people with influence to help me.

In June last year, there were only about a hundred learners attending the tutorship programme. Now, Sibusiso and his mates tutor up to 700 learners.

TRACY: These values don't just help them at school, it actually helps them after school, 81% of them after school are in university, further educational studying or volunteering if they haven't managed to find a job.

And this makes them highly employable, says outsourcing company Merchants’ people director, Jennifer Algie.
Several Columba learners have been employed as first-time employees by Merchants.

JENNIFER ALGIE: They believe in themselves, so they are confident what is not to be underestimated, they learn to thrive in the school environment, they teach them to fish, when they come into our environments, they stand out

Columba’s goal is that by 2020, 12-thousand young leaders would have graduated from its leadership programme and they in turn, would have mobilised large numbers of additional learners from their schools.

TRACY: I get excited about the future for South Africa interacting with these quality quality young people.

SIBU: I want to be in a place where everyone is equal in as far as social and economic and political factors are concerned. My mission is to get my degree and get the capitol to give back to my community.






PROMO’S

PROMO 1:15”

DEVI: South Africa has one of worst unemployment rates in the world. We bring you a story of a leadership program that is making a difference.

TRACY: 81% of them after school are in university, further educational studying or volunteering if they haven't managed to find a job.

PROMO 2: 15”

TRACY: I get excited about the future for South Africa interacting with these quality quality young people.

SIBU: I want to be in a place where everyone is equal.

A leadership program changes the way learners think encouraging them to succeed.

PROMO 3: 10”

South Africa has one of the highest youth unemployment rates in the world. Something has to change?
TRACY: I sometimes feel the way in which we are interacting with the youth is the solution.

SIBU: Not everyone will get the chance to be part of Columba. It’s all about passion. Start by setting your own goals. Be specific and realistic. I would go for people with influence to help me. In June last year, there were only about a hundred learners attending the tutorship programme. Now, Sibusiso and his mates tutor up to 700 learners. metadata.Summary: SA has a youth unemployment rate of 60%, the third highest in the world. Change doesn't happen overnight, but at least one organisation is trying to change the values of learners to become future leaders. In 2011, we did a story about Columba1400SA - an Academy that teaches young people to change the way they think. This leadership development program was founded by high-profile Scottish cleric and leadership Norman Drummond in Scotland in 1997 and brought to South Africa in 2009 by businessman Rob Taylor. When we did the story in 2011, they have had 350 learners who graduated successfully under this programme introduced into mostly rural and disadvantaged schools, working on a selection system. Now they already have 3500 graduates.
metadata.Further information: Too many young people drop out before completing high school, not having something to look forward to after completing school. Most of them that do complete matric, leave ill-prepared for life after school and more often than not, become part of the 60% unemployment statistic for young people between the ages of 18 and 35. A lack of skills and a good value system while in school contribute to this high youth unemployment figure. Unemployment traps people in poverty and potentially also contribute to instability in the country. Columba 1400SA has a mission to build a national movement of engaged young leaders for youth employment and school improvement and they offer a values-based leadership programme to schools that challenge learners, not only to become the best they can be, to think out of the box,. to have a future vision, to be motivated and determined, but also to inspire others and lead by example in getting a society together in order to uplift their own communities. The system works on selective basis. Learners have to write essays on the changes they want to see in themselves, their community and their schools. High-achievers and troublemakers are included in the mix and taught values such as perseverance, creativity, relationship and leadership, planning and problem solving, managing feelings, resilience and determination and integrity to elevate their ideals in life beyond just self-interest to examine projects with social and environmental significance. Columba activate the potential of a small core group of learners and adults (the principal and educators, maybe some adults in the community) to lead positive change. This group in turn spend two years recruiting, mobilising and engaging large numbers of their peers and implementing ongoing social impact projects and these projects provide numerous opportunities for learners to develop a range of skills and capabilities. 75% of the Columba graduates being tracked are in higher of further education programmes studying or working within two years of leaving school. Columba's mission is to activate a national movement of engaged young leaders to improve their schools and youth employment. In six years, Columba has developed more than 2400 leaders in 90 schools in seven provinces. They have mobilised over 40 000 beneficiaries with 21st century skills, such as foundational literacies (how students apply core skills to everyday tasks like literacy, numeracy, scientific literacy, ICT literacy, financial literacy and cultural and civic literacy), competencies (how students approach complex challenges like critical thinking and problem solving, creativity, communication and collaboration) and character qualities (how students approach their changing environment like curiosity, initiative, persistence/grit, adaptability, leadership and social and cultural awareness). The impact on the individual is that that learner is more future orientated, inspired for education, self-confident and committed to social contribution. 81% of Columba graduates are studying with the help of bursaries, working or volunteering after leaving school - ultimately narrowing the gap of South Africa's 60% young unemployment rate for people between the ages of 18 and 35. The effect these changes value systems and endorsed programmes have on schools are enormously successful - of participating principals, 100% report improved culture of learning in the school, 90% report it made their role and that of other educators easier and 100% would recommend the program to other schools for its relevance and empowering outcomes. In schools there is a strong positive impact on academic performance, school drop-outs, teen pregnancy, classroom discipline, late coming and absenteeism. In the 2011 story, we introduced the Columba 1400SA programme to our viewers. Although we will still be saying in this story what Columba is and what they do and still go to three schools in Thaba Nchu outside Bloemfontein where we will speak to one very inspiring learner at one of Thaba Nchu's more rural schools (she is making a massive impact on her school and community as an individual, but also as part of her small group), we will be speaking to a principal and teacher at another school in Thaba Nchu where the results over the past years have been enormous and at another school in Thaba Nchu, we will be focusing on the small group of learners who are part of the Columba programme and making huge strides in their community - they even started a feeding scheme for the primary school, getting their own sponsors and the Free State education department followed on and is now providing this Primary School with a feeding scheme every day. In Johannesburg we will be interviewing the CEO of Columba on the changes since our last story and the impact they are making, and we will interview two Columba Alumni's - Caroline, who has had a complete 360 turn-around in her life because of the Columba leadership programme in 2011 and is now studying chemical engineering, and Solly, who became involved in gansterism before he even turned ten, and also had a complete turnaround in his life because of the programme - he said he only wanted to join Columba to make trouble, then realised what he could make of his life. He graduated matric with four distinctions, is now working at a FET college and studying law through Unisa. The three learners we have interviewed in our 2011 story, are all three still based in KZN. I will only mention in the new story what they do now and where they work - how their lives have progressed since.
